facts: Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American from Michigan who had been living in Ukraine, was released by Russia after being detained since 2022 and sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in a penal colony on accusations of fighting for a Ukrainian defense unit.

Hubbard was released on Wednesday and arrived back in the U.S. at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio early Thursday; he was reported to be in poor health and expected to receive treatment in Texas.
The release occurred as Trump special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg; Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin acted for humanitarian reasons.
President Trump said he personally asked Putin to free Hubbard during talks on settling the Ukraine war and that no prisoner swap was required.
After the release, Witkoff publicly called Putin a 'humanitarian,' prompting criticism from Republican lawmakers including Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.), Rep. Don Bacon, and Sen. John Cornyn.
Vice President JD Vance defended Witkoff, saying his job was to secure the release and that he cared less about Witkoff's wording than about bringing an American home.
The State Department said the release was welcome and that there are currently no Americans classified as wrongfully detained in Russia.

Separately, Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and waived newly enacted sanctions on Russian officials, banks, and state enterprises, while increasing pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced.
ladder.analysis: Hubbard's release came as Trump special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg, with Trump saying he had personally asked Putin to free Hubbard as part of talks on settling the Ukraine war. The episode unfolded alongside other Russia-related policy moves—including eased sanctions and a new diesel import deal—that have drawn scrutiny in Washington. Witkoff's decision to call Putin a 'humanitarian' after the release sparked criticism from several Republican lawmakers, while the administration defended the envoy's focus on securing the release of a detained American over the specific language he used.
ladder.steelman: The episode highlights a tension between the administration's focus on securing concrete outcomes, such as Hubbard's release, and criticism from lawmakers over the rhetoric used toward Putin during the process.
ladder.implications: The backlash from Republican lawmakers signals potential friction for the Trump administration as it pursues further diplomacy with Russia, particularly as sanctions relief and envoy rhetoric face continued congressional scrutiny ahead of the midterms.

facts: On Monday, White House Counsel William Scharf sent a letter to Politico Global Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger demanding retraction and apology for three articles about Trump and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, warning Politico to retract or 'face the consequences.'

The three disputed articles were: an Oct. 15 Playbook piece headlined 'Trump's ice maiden is under fire' suggesting Trump sought to replace Wiles; an Oct. 16 Playbook piece describing a West Wing 'freakout' and claiming Trump 'blew up'; and an Oct. 17 story alleging Wiles arranged ousted press secretary Katie Zacharia's Fox News interview with Sean Hannity.
Politico issued a correction on Wednesday to the Oct. 17 story, stating its 'follow-up reporting indicates she did not play a direct role in setting up the interview.'

Politico's attorneys responded to Scharf on Wednesday, rejecting the White House's claims as false and accusing the administration of a 'pattern of unconstitutional conduct' intended to intimidate the outlet.

Politico, CNN and MS NOW were barred from White House grounds in September; U.S. District Judge Tim Kelly ruled the removal was likely unconstitutional and ordered access reinstated. Politico was separately barred from boarding Air Force One earlier in October.

This week Trump told Independent correspondent Andrew Feinberg in the Oval Office 'you better be careful,' called him a 'sick person,' and Feinberg was later removed from the traveling press pool for a trip to Iowa with little notice.
Trump also called CNN's Kaitlan Collins a 'low-IQ person' and 'dummy' over a question about Russia sanctions, and asked an ABC News reporter, 'Are you a stupid person?'
The White House Correspondents' Association characterized the administration's actions toward reporters this week as 'retaliation,' according to a Deadline report cited by the Washington Post.
ladder.analysis: This story centers on an escalating standoff between the Trump White House and the press corps, combining a formal legal threat against Politico with a string of public confrontations involving individual reporters from The Independent, CNN and ABC News. The dispute with Politico follows a now-familiar pattern: the outlet published reporting the White House disputed, one story was partially corrected, and the administration responded not just with denials but with an explicit threat of legal and access consequences — raising questions about the line between holding media accountable for errors and using government power to pressure news organizations. The broader context includes a September ban on Politico, CNN and MS NOW from White House grounds that a federal judge found likely unconstitutional, and a separate restriction barring Politico from Air Force One earlier in October, showing access disputes have already drawn judicial scrutiny once this year.
ladder.steelman: The episode exposes a genuine tension rather than a one-sided scandal: Politico's own correction shows at least one story contained a real inaccuracy the White House was justified in flagging, while the administration's response — legal threats, access bans found likely unconstitutional, and personal insults toward individual reporters — raises separate concerns about whether corrections are being used as a pretext for broader press intimidation.
ladder.implications: Watch for whether Politico faces further access restrictions or legal action, whether courts are asked again to rule on press-access bans as they did in September, and whether other outlets alter their reporting or defend Politico publicly, all of which will shape how future disputes between this White House and the press corps over accuracy and access are resolved.

The order was brief and unsigned, giving no explanation.

stories.headline: Houthi attack kills two at Saudi airport; US evacuates staff, oil surges amid Iran tensions
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Two people were killed on Wednesday evening in a Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, Saudi authorities said. The General Authority of Civil Aviation identified the victims as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident. The Iran-backed Houthis claimed the airport was among targets they struck with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours. The U.S. State Department subsequently ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to depart Saudi Arabia, citing escalating Houthi hostilities against the kingdom, including attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.

Earlier Wednesday, two more people — residents from the Philippines and Nepal — were killed by debris from a drone intercepted over Eastern Province as it attempted to target an Aramco processing facility at the Shaybah oil field, according to the Saudi energy ministry. A contractor’s vehicle was set ablaze. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four drones over Eastern Province on Wednesday night and four more over Riyadh and Medina provinces on Thursday. At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since October, according to Saudi authorities.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for Saudi air strikes on territory they control in western Yemen. Houthi-run media reported at least six killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours. The war in Yemen, which began in 2014 when the Houthis ousted the internationally recognized government, escalated in 2015 with a Saudi-led intervention. An informal ceasefire unraveled in July when the Houthis announced a “maritime embargo” and began targeting Saudi airports, oil facilities and Red Sea tankers. In September, the Houthis seized part of Yemen’s southwestern coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a global shipping chokepoint, contributing to rising oil prices.

The U.S. military has also quietly reduced its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats from the Houthis and Iran, officials told CBS News. The U.S. and Israel are planning for a possible attack on Iran in early November, after the U.S. midterm elections, a person briefed on war planning told NPR. Iran’s foreign minister said, “We are just as prepared for diplomacy as we are for war.”  The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced a shift to an “offensive and asymmetrical” defense doctrine, threatening to invade neighboring countries that launch attacks against Iran. IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, and that it is preparing to unveil the “father of all bombs.”

Brent crude oil climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said it struck four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Gulf, and three other vessels hit mines west of the Strait of Hormuz. The International Monetary Fund warned that if the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continues and energy supply disruptions persist, oil will average $130 a barrel in 2027. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom has offered to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, as the conflict threatens to draw in wider regional powers.

Analysts warned that renewed confrontation between the U.S., Israel and Iran is increasingly possible. Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that Iran wants to establish a new equation: “Any future attack on Iran will come at a much higher cost for the aggressors.”  Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, seeking reelection, has campaigned on a pledge to topple Iran’s government. U.S. President Donald Trump said this week that “we are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon,” while also saying Washington could end the war immediately but wants a lasting outcome.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine trade missile and drone strikes after agreeing to resume peace talks
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Russia and Ukraine traded missile and drone strikes overnight, hours after Moscow agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks. Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv in three waves, hitting several houses; Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said six people were injured, while Al Jazeera reported 15 wounded in the capital. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones toward Moscow, with Russian officials reporting tallies of intercepted or downed drones varying from 163 to more than 800, and Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said two people were wounded near the capital.

The agreement to resume the three-way talks came after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday, a day after Witkoff met Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Norway and Finland in Oslo. “The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we’re getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we’ve been,” President Donald Trump said. Zelenskyy said the Oslo discussions covered “strong” security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said a new round — the first since the talks were paused in February — could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi and must focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict.” He cautioned, however, that the Americans’ ideas were not very “useful” and that “these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us.”

Zelenskyy said he hoped negotiations would begin early in November, and told Fox News he would accept a deal freezing the war along the current front line. “We call it ‘ceasefire’ or ‘stop killings’ like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today,” he said, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed afterward. Russia has said it will not end the fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances — terms Kyiv dismisses as a demand for capitulation. Putin launched the full-scale invasion in 2022, and Moscow controls about 20 percent of Ukrainian territory; Ushakov said Putin had told Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere and held the “strategic initiative,” a claim Ukraine and its European allies dispute, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

Despite the diplomatic movement, both sides kept up their long-range attacks. Russia said it carried out a “massive strike” overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine’s Odesa region and on vessels used by the Ukrainian military; in Russia’s Belgorod border region, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said. The two sides also conducted an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to Belarus’s Belta state news agency — the kind of step that has accompanied moves toward talks in the past. The war has now ground on for more than four and a half years, defying Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge that he could end it in a day; no breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year or from three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year.

The renewed push came amid sharp friction between Kyiv and Washington. Ukraine says the US has withheld early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the Starlink satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile-defense systems bought on its behalf by Europeans; Washington denies any deliberate policy shift. US officials have denied requesting a Starlink slowdown, and a bipartisan group of senators has called for an urgent investigation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the intelligence allegations as “scandalous,” and Zelenskyy said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing “works now.” Trump, who has called for Zelenskyy to be replaced and said Russia’s actions in Ukraine have been “fine,” has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. He also lifted sanctions on Russia — allowing it to release diesel “to the American and global marketplace” — a move criticized by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers.

Witkoff’s visit also produced the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American who had been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for allegedly fighting on Ukraine’s behalf. Trump said Hubbard was “on his way back home” and that “there was no ‘swap’ necessary,” while Witkoff thanked Putin, calling him a “humanitarian.” Vice President JD Vance defended that description: “I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family.” Zelenskyy mocked the label on X, writing: “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles.” He said two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions. Witkoff called the talks “constructive,” while Trump adviser Jared Kushner, joining by video link, said: “There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come.”

body: North Korea said it would put propaganda loudspeakers along the entire border with South Korea on standby within days and begin broadcasting from some time in October, a move that would mark the first cross-border loudspeaker exchange in 16 months. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, made the announcement in a statement carried by the state news agency KCNA, a day after she first said the loudspeakers would operate along the whole border.

Speaking after a border inspection with Marshal Pak Jong-chon, an adviser to Pyongyang's defence ministry, Kim — her brother's top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul — said North Korea's "tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," using the initials of South Korea's formal name, the Republic of Korea. She also said "new counter means" would be placed on alert, and described the border as "clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly." Calling the fortification work a "sacred and great undertaking" supporting Kim Jong-un's policy of permanently severing ties with the South, she quoted the leader as saying the border "should be a permanent line never to be crossed." KCNA initially reported the inspection as occurring Tuesday; Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said routine maintenance of the North's loudspeakers had been observed before her statements.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August. If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. Seoul's Defense Ministry spokesperson, Chung Binna, said Thursday that if North Korea went ahead, "naturally there would have to be a proportional measure," but made clear no decision had been made. Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Jin Yong-Sung called Kim's threats "intolerable" and ordered the military to "sternly respond" to potential provocations.

Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously. Seoul and the U.S.-led United Nations Command, which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean War, concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a "self-staged farce."

Since Kim Jong-un declared in December 2023 that the two Koreas were "two states hostile to each other," North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border. Seoul says North Korean soldiers have crossed the military demarcation line 50 times this year during the fortification work, prompting South Korean troops to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots; the North has dismissed those claims as a "false pretext" and called the broadcasts and shots provocations by "armed rogues." Kim Yo-jong warned that if South Korean warning shots caused "actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons' safety," North Korean border guards "will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason."

The standoff comes amid a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations between Pyongyang and Washington, with Kim Jong-un having cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with the South and declared it a permanent enemy. The two Koreas have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border — the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls and the South airing K-pop music and news criticizing Pyongyang. During the border inspection, Pak Jong-chon accused the South of making "deliberate, premeditated and absurd" claims to shift blame over the rising tensions, denied that North Korean troops had breached the border, and threatened an "overwhelming response" to provocations.

stories.headline: Macron blames far-left for unrest, bans protests in Paris and other cities
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has blamed far-left groups for stoking violence during weekend protests, as authorities banned demonstrations in several major cities including Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble. Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests and gripped Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Nice. At least 2,500 people were arrested after shops were looted and property destroyed, with the government admitting police had "lost control" during the violence.

Speaking from the Elysee Palace on Thursday, Macron accused "ultra-left" groups of committing "seditious acts" and trying to "bring down the Republic." He vowed the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups," which he blamed for much of the trouble. The Paris Police Prefecture announced that Thursday's protests would be banned in key parts of the city until 8pm, including areas near the presidential palace, both houses of parliament, main train stations, and parts of downtown where looting occurred. A police source told AFP the ban was necessary due to organisers' "inability to prevent violence and vandalism." Authorities also prohibited protests planned for Thursday in Lyon, Lille and Grenoble, and some Saturday marches, including in Lyon, will be banned.

Macron also accused unnamed foreign leaders of exploiting the riots for electoral purposes, saying they were campaigning "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence. Speaking in Doha, he said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders... We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false." The comments appeared to be aimed at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month. On Tuesday, Netanyahu said France had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam," while Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration, saying "close your borders and take control before it is too late!"

According to the Financial Times, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots. Unnamed security officials said pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging. David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university, said "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives." BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka. The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24. Separately, BBC Verify traced one of the most viral AI-generated images, supposedly showing an elderly couple being robbed in Paris, to an obscure website. The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team created the image using ChatGPT without a reference image; it was later shared on X without a disclaimer, attracting more than six million views.

The education demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff, and spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. The school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs. More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday in a protest that brought together students and groups denouncing high living costs. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a "massive" security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence. Macron said he would convene the country's defence council on Friday to take further action. Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals; they are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled for November 5, calling on private and public sector employees to join.

stories.headline: Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard as Witkoff and Putin discuss Ukraine peace plan
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of jailed American Stephen Hubbard during talks Wednesday with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Putin said the 74-year-old Michigan native was already at the airport, and Witkoff said Hubbard was now "going home to his family." President Donald Trump later said he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week and insisted the U.S. gave nothing in return, writing on Truth Social that "there was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

Hubbard, a former schoolteacher, was taken captive by Russian forces in eastern Ukraine in 2022 after moving there following his marriage to a Ukrainian woman. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024 on mercenary charges he denies, and the U.S. formally designated him wrongfully detained under the Biden administration. State media footage showed a smiling Hubbard shaking hands with Witkoff, and his son, Orthodox priest Father Joseph Coleman, thanked both Trump and Putin. Trump also acknowledged that suspending a new round of sanctions had been a necessary concession, saying, "If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt."

The release came during the ninth meeting between Witkoff and Putin, which centered on a potential settlement of the nearly 4 1/2-year war in Ukraine. Witkoff said he had brought "some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine" for Putin to review. The Kremlin said the proposals "lacked substance" and would not be of real use, but Putin agreed "in principle" to resume trilateral peace talks with Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. delegates after November 10, with his foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov saying such talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends." Ushakov added that a possible first-ever meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the United States in Beijing "is being prepared."

Hubbard's release followed a series of recent U.S. gestures toward Moscow against the backdrop of the negotiations. Trump has agreed to buy previously sanctioned Russian diesel fuel, placed a waiver on a congressional sanctions package he had signed into law, pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil facilities and called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's ouster. Putin, meanwhile, announced that the first shipments of Russian diesel, 60,000 tons, would head to the U.S. in the coming days. The White House has framed the engagement with Russia as part of a wider plan to keep Moscow involved in peace negotiations and in the interest of American consumers.

Zelenskyy, who met Witkoff in Norway a day before the St. Petersburg talks, called Wednesday for freezing the front line as a first step toward ceasefire negotiations. "Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," he said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin was supporting Ukraine to end the war as quickly as possible, adding that any capitulation by Ukraine would be "a capitulation by all of us." The European Union, which had delegates from several member states at the Oslo talks on Tuesday, said it expected to be debriefed by Washington after Wednesday's meeting.

Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said, adding, "I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy." While the Kremlin's agreement to revive trilateral talks marked a shift after Putin had refused such discussions, its characterization of Witkoff's proposals as lacking substance left open the question of whether the renewed process would yield concrete progress toward ending the war.

stories.headline: Meta earnings beat overshadowed by rising AI spending and nonvoting share overhang
body: Meta reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, with revenue of $64.6 billion—a 26% increase from a year ago and above the $63.37 billion analysts had expected—and GAAP earnings per share of $3.83, beating the $3.56 consensus estimate. The company also issued strong guidance for the current period, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, with a midpoint of $74.5 billion that topped the $73.73 billion analysts projected. The stock initially rose about 2.5% in extended trading after the release, but fell 2% in premarket trading Thursday as other concerns weighed on investors.

The strong quarter was powered by Meta's core advertising business, which benefited from AI-driven recommendations, higher ad volume, and rising ad prices. CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the launch of Muse and Muse Wonder, Meta's first frontier model, as major milestones toward delivering 'personal superintelligence for everyone.' The Muse AI personal assistant, which debuted in September, helped Meta end the month with its best performance on Wall Street since 2022. Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and updates at a rapid pace, including Muse Wonder, released last Monday.

However, the positive earnings news was overshadowed by Meta's announcement that it is creating a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock, effectively a 2-for-1 stock split. Under the plan, existing shareholders will receive one nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they hold, with trading slated to begin in January 2027. The move is designed in part to keep founder Mark Zuckerberg working in California as the 5% billionaire's tax looms, and it allows him to raise external capital for Meta's AI build-out without diluting his personal voting control over the company.

Wall Street reacted negatively to the unexpected overhang. JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth advised Meta to issue the stock quickly so that focus can return to the company's product momentum. 'The sooner the better in our view as it would remove the overhang and the Street now knows it will have non-voting shares in Jan'27, and Meta can still do a substantial equity raise before then without even coming close to impacting Mark's voting control,' Anmuth said. He added that despite 'some near-term noise in Meta shares,' he is encouraged by the core advertising business, the outlook for strong overall revenue growth in 2027, and the increasingly clear path to superintelligence with the Muse series of models and products.

The combination of rising AI spending anxiety—exacerbated by similar concerns after Tesla's earnings—and the new nonvoting share overhang contributed to a slide in AI stocks following the reports. Meta's stock decline in premarket trading reflected investor unease even as the company posted a revenue beat and strong guidance. The tension between Meta's promising new AI businesses and the financial mechanics of funding them without ceding control underscores the challenges facing the company as it pursues its ambitious AI agenda.

stories.headline: Tesla beats earnings estimates but lowered capex target raises AI and robotics doubts
body: Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue declined. The company posted adjusted earnings per share of 48 cents, beating the 43-cent estimate from analysts polled by LSEG, while revenue came in at $28.05 billion against a $27.9 billion forecast. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading.

Automotive revenue fell 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion, and energy revenue dropped 16% to $2.88 billion. Offsetting those declines, services and other revenue climbed 33% to $4.61 billion. Net income attributable to common shareholders plunged 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier. Tesla attributed the weaker automotive results to lower average sales prices and trouble securing battery supplies to fulfill a backlog of orders.

The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion, and free cash flow fell 62% year over year to $1.53 billion after turning negative in the second quarter.

Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised) partially automated driving system, sold for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million. Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) system around the second quarter of next year. On the robotaxi front, CEO Elon Musk said the driverless fleet, which now includes 362 Model Y and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, will start to contribute to financials in 2027, though he added it could become noticeable by the second quarter of next year and a big deal by the third or fourth quarter.

The earnings report came a day after Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a 'good idea' for his two companies to merge and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. 'I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield,' Musk said on that call, responding to a question about a potential merger. On the Tesla call, he said only, 'I think I said everything that should be said yesterday.' Tesla is also building a semiconductor factory with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas, and the companies have other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, intensifying speculation about a combination.

On Optimus, Musk said the company is 'making good progress' on the AI systems that control the robots but that there is 'still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.' He expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be 'solved around the end of next year.' Tesla reported vehicle deliveries of 486,532 for the quarter, about 2% below the year-ago number. The company said auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records, though it has seen meager growth in its core market as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gain popularity in Asia and Europe.

stories.headline: Carrick's job under threat after Man Utd's humbling by Como; Fernandes criticises tactics
body: Michael Carrick is set to remain in charge of Manchester United for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, but senior figures at the club are increasingly concerned by performances and results after Wednesday's humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Italian side Como. The loss extended United's winless run to seven matches in all competitions, their worst such streak since 2015-16. United have won just two of their 11 games this season, with only one clean sheet kept across all fixtures.

After the defeat, captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics, telling TNT Sports: "It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence." Asked if Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes replied: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me." Carrick responded by saying: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Fernandes' comments have drawn widespread criticism. Former Liverpool vice-captain Jamie Carragher called his attitude "an absolute disgrace" and "not what a Manchester United captain should be", while former Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole described the public questioning as "sacrilege". Former Leicester and Celtic goalkeeper Kasper Schmeichel said Fernandes "probably should not be saying these things because it's only going to add to the problems". The outburst follows similar remarks from defender Lisandro Martinez after a previous defeat, for which he later apologised.

Despite the mounting pressure, Carrick is expected to remain in charge for Sunday's match, with United's hierarchy divided over whether a change would help. Some believe the squad, which one source described as a "Champions League squad", should be performing far better, while others note that chopping and changing managers in recent years has failed to arrest the club's decline. United have already begun identifying possible replacements, with Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Nagelsmann all understood to be interested in the role. Aston Villa's Unai Emery and Brighton's Fabian Hurzeler are also highly regarded but would be difficult to extract from their current clubs.

The team have been hampered by injuries and a lack of form, with players failing to reach expected levels. Accusations of a lack of passion, desire and intensity have dogged United all season. The proximity of Sunday's Premier League game makes an immediate change difficult, but a clear midweek following their EFL Cup exit could provide time for the hierarchy to take stock. United have yet to confirm arrangements for Friday's planned news conference to preview the Bournemouth match, adding to the sense of uncertainty that continues to surround the club.

stories.headline: World Series preview: Rays vs. Brewers – key factors and predictions
body: The top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays (98 wins) will face the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers (103 wins) in the World Series, beginning Friday at 8 p.m. ET in Milwaukee. Neither franchise has ever won a World Series title. The Rays swept the Yankees in the ALDS and rallied from a 2-1 deficit to beat the Guardians in the ALCS, while the Brewers lost just one game this postseason, sweeping the back-to-back champion Dodgers in the NLCS after dispatching the Padres.

Though the Brewers are favored – they won more regular-season games, posted a better run differential, and faced a tougher schedule – the Rays may have an edge at the front of the rotation. Tampa Bay's Drew Rasmussen and ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta have a 1.19 ERA and 3.50 K/BB ratio in 37⅔ postseason innings, compared to Milwaukee's Jacob Misiorowski (NL Cy Young favorite) and Logan Henderson, who have a combined 3.12 ERA and 1.89 K/BB in 17⅓ innings. There are concerns that the younger Brewers arms are hitting a workload wall: Misiorowski's combined innings jumped from 141⅓ in 2025 to 183 this season, and Henderson's from 103 to 131⅓. Rasmussen and Peralta are older and more experienced with high workloads.

The Rays have been a different team since the trade deadline, going 40-20 (including 7-2 in the playoffs). Key additions include Peralta, who posted a 131 ERA+ in 10 starts after being acquired from the Mets; catcher Liam Hicks, who batted .288/.379/.440 for Tampa Bay and became Kevin Cash's No. 3 hitter; and right-handed reliever Tyler Wells, who improved the setup depth.

Junior Caminero is the best hitter in the series, according to sources. The 22-year-old third baseman played in every game this season, posting a 144 OPS+ with 42 homers after hitting 45 in 2025. He has top-tier quality-of-contact indicators and is the most likely player to take over a game or series with his bat. However, he has not yet erupted in the postseason, entering the ALCS clincher 7-for-30 with two RBI and three extra-base hits before his Game 6 homer.

In position-by-position matchups, the Brewers hold edges at catcher (William Contreras, who leads all LCS players with a 1.157 OPS this postseason) and first base (Jake Bauers, NLCS MVP and the best hitter on baseball's best team during the regular season). At second base, Brice Turang is a sensational defender with a well-rounded offensive game. At shortstop, the Rays' Taylor Walls is the best defensive shortstop in the sport, while Milwaukee's rookie Cooper Pratt has impressed with his arm and contact hitting. In left field, Chandler Simpson's slash-and-dash style is unique, but Jackson Chourio remains dangerous despite a .171/.211/.343 line in October.

The World Series pits two teams that have never won a title, with the Rays as underdogs despite a 98-win season. As one source notes, 'underdog does not mean fated to lose,' and a Rays series win would be barely a mild upset. The outcome may hinge on the front-of-rotation duel, Caminero's bat, and whether Milwaukee's young arms can sustain their performance through a potentially long series.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind staff quit over military AI contracts
body: Several staff members have resigned from Google DeepMind, Google's artificial intelligence laboratory, in protest over the company's military AI contracts with the U.S. and Israeli governments. Research engineer Sofia Liguori resigned this week, telling the BBC she felt ashamed to work at Google after realizing the company was pushing for AI systems in military operations. AI researcher Andreas Kirsch also resigned earlier this month, citing insufficient governance and oversight to deploy AI safely in classified military settings. The departures follow Google's signing of a contract earlier this year allowing its AI technology to be used for classified U.S. military work, as well as its involvement in Project Nimbus, a $1.2 billion joint contract with Amazon providing Israel's government and military with AI and cloud computing infrastructure.

Liguori, a London-based research engineer who joined DeepMind in 2023, said she initially believed the company would have a net positive impact on society. In an internal resignation letter, she wrote: 'I no longer believe that our technology will have a net positive impact on society. I think there’s a fantasy world where AI can help decarbonize grids, cut waste, protect ecosystems, and benefit humanity. But it’s not this world, and it’s not this type of general purpose AI we are racing to develop.' She told the BBC that her employment contract restricted her from publicly criticizing Google, but she chose to speak out because she believes it is important for these issues to be known. She added that staff are scared of retaliation and putting their careers at risk, and that they feel watched and unable to speak.

Kirsch told the BBC he believes 'Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings' and that 'Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed.' The Pentagon has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority, with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth saying the Trump administration will become an 'AI-first warfighting force.' The U.S. military has deployed AI-enabled technologies such as Maven Smart Systems, a Palantir-developed platform that uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, former director of Project Maven, said the philosophy appears to be: 'Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation.'

Current and former staff have raised concerns about the level of human oversight in AI-driven military operations. Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team, said: 'AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment. When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors.' Google's contract with the Pentagon states its AI models should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons without appropriate human oversight and control, but critics question whether such safeguards are sufficient. A current Google DeepMind employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that 'a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of their careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard.'

Google has defended its approach, with a spokesperson telling the BBC: 'We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles. We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind.' The company's AI Principles include implementing AI with 'human oversight' and aligning the technology with 'international law and human rights.' However, Liguori and other departing staff have expressed doubt that these principles are being upheld in practice, particularly as the U.S. military pushes to deploy AI as quickly as possible across battlefield operations, transport, and planning.

stories.headline: Tesla profit drops 43% as Optimus production begins and Cybercab sales planned
body: Tesla reported a 43 percent drop in net profit for the third quarter of 2026, falling to $787 million, even as the company announced early production of its Optimus humanoid robot and plans to sell its autonomous Cybercab to customers by the end of the year. Revenue for the quarter was $28 billion, nearly flat year over year, while automotive revenue slipped 3 percent to $20.6 billion. Operating expenses rose 39 percent to $4.8 billion, pushing the company's operating margin down to 2.6 percent from 5.8 percent a year earlier. Capital expenditures more than doubled, increasing 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow fell 62 percent to $1.5 billion.

On the company's earnings call Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk said Tesla had begun early production of its humanoid robot, Optimus, on its high-volume line in Fremont, California. Musk described the machines coming off the line as 'production-quality bots' but acknowledged substantial unfinished work. 'There's still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks,' Musk said. He noted that the robot's hands are not yet perfected, and that durability, reliability, and safety remain challenges. 'It can't, like, wear out after a month,' Musk said. Tesla did not disclose how many robots it has produced, what tasks they can perform autonomously, or how often they complete those tasks without human intervention.

Musk said the company needs to build roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practice tasks at what he called 'Optimus Academy,' generating training data through self-play. He compared the process to a toddler learning skills gradually. Tesla is also waiting on its AI5 chip, which Musk hopes to integrate around April 2027 and which would provide roughly 10 times the computing power of the current AI4 chip. Musk expects the pieces to come together around the end of 2027, when Tesla could begin delivering Optimus to outside companies, though he did not specify which companies or what the robots would do for them. Most of the equipment for a line intended to produce a million robots annually is already in Fremont, Musk said, but reaching a rate of 20,000 robots a week will take 'at least a year, maybe a little longer.'

Ken Goldberg, a robotics professor at the University of California, Berkeley, told The Verge that producing hardware without the software to make it useful is a significant problem. 'If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that's a big problem,' Goldberg said. He noted that dexterity remains a particularly hard challenge and that task success rates in robotics labs have stalled at around 70 to 80 percent. 'That's not acceptable for real industry,' he said. Musk promised a video within a month or two showing Optimus performing tasks that are not preprogrammed, criticizing humanoid demonstrations that look impressive but would not translate into useful real-world performance. 'If you actually try to use that humanoid robot in the real world, you would have a lot of trouble,' he said. 'It wouldn't work, basically.'

Separately, Tesla said it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets safety standards. The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls. During the earnings call, Tesla vice president of engineering Lars Moravy said Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company's own robotaxi fleet, and that the company will 'mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers' as the fleet grows, starting small. Tesla first floated the idea of selling the autonomous vehicle to third parties last month and posted a form for interested buyers, but it was not clear how the company would follow through.

Musk said the Cybercab is primarily a ride-hailing vehicle, not a car for personal ownership. 'Cybercab is primarily going to be something that is offered as like transport as a service,' Musk said, adding that the vast majority of Cybercabs will be Tesla-owned and operated as a service. Musk also said an unsupervised version of Full Self-Driving would be rolled out to customers sometime in the second quarter of next year, another delay for Tesla owners who have subscribed to or bought the software. If both timelines hold, third-party fleet customers would be able to buy the autonomous Cybercab and potentially operate it as a robotaxi service before Tesla owners get access to the same autonomous capability in their own cars. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into the Cybercab last month, just hours after the vehicles began operating on public streets in Austin.
